title: Short Stuff: Hisashi Ouchi
summary: Short Stuff episode on the 1999 Tokaimura nuclear accident (criticality accident) at the JCO fuel-processing plant in Tokaimura, Japan. Covers the unapproved shortcut procedure of pouring uranium solution into a precipitation tank, the uncontrolled chain reaction lasting about 20 hours, and the 17-sievert exposure to worker Hisashi Ouchi. Discusses his treatment (blood transfusions, stem cell transplant from his sister, failed bone marrow recovery), his death on December 21, 1999 after 83 days, the death of second-closest worker Masato Shinohara in April 2000, and the aftermath: JCO officials' suspended sentences in 2003, fines, loss of license, and regulatory reform.
topics: Stuff You Should Know short stuff

segments.title: Introduction
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the sad Short Stuff episode about the Tokaimura nuclear accident and victim Hisashi Ouchi.

segments.title: What happened at Tokaimura
segments.summary: JCO workers were dissolving uranium oxide and, under an unapproved shortcut, poured oversized amounts of uranium solution into a precipitation tank on September 30, 1999. This reached criticality and produced a self-sustaining chain reaction with intense neutron and gamma radiation for about 20 hours until emergency workers drained the cooling jacket and added boric acid. Ouchi received an estimated 17 sieverts; he was called the most radioactive man in history, though he was not a radiation risk to others.

segments.title: Radiation dose discussion
segments.summary: Josh checks the radiation units, comparing the dose to chest X-ray exposure, and notes his surprise that Ouchi survived the initial exposure long enough to suffer over 83 days.

segments.title: Ouchi's medical decline and treatment
segments.summary: The radiation shattered chromosomes and damaged fast-dividing cells, starting with the gut lining, skin and bone marrow. Ouchi was moved from a local hospital to the National Institute of Radiological Sciences in Chiba and then to University of Tokyo Hospital. Doctors tried blood transfusions and stem cell transplants, including a bone marrow donation from his sister, but the transplanted cells were also damaged. He suffered skin and intestinal failure, needed fluid replacement and respiratory support, and organ failure set in.

segments.title: Deaths and public reaction
segments.summary: Masato Shinohara, the second-closest worker, died in April 2000. Ouchi died December 21, 1999, 83 days after the blast. The case drew wide news coverage and exposed JCO's poor practices.

segments.title: JCO failures and aftermath
segments.summary: JCO allowed shortcuts, lacked regulatory approval, provided little safety training, had no criticality alarm, and conducted few inspections. The third worker survived. The IAEA blamed human error and safety breaches. In 2003, six officials received suspended prison sentences for professional negligence, the company was fined, and it lost its license, reportedly a first in Japan. Safety inspectors were also faulted, and Japan strengthened nuclear regulation.

segments.title: Closing
segments.summary: Hosts reflect that the accident led to improved safety practices, then sign off.
